summary:
Queensland is a state within Australia and stands under the national framework, while carrying its own layer of gender-identity law. Amendments to the Anti-Discrimination Act commenced on 29 April 2024, moving serious vilification out of that Act and into the Criminal Code with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity, as stated by the Queensland Human Rights Commission. The Queensland Human Rights Commission separately announced stronger discrimination protections for gender-diverse people as part of an Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 rewrite, describing a modernised 'gender identity' attribute and revised vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to enact a criminal ban on conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the Queensland parliament on 13 August 2020, criminalising practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity, with fines and jail time for practitioners; the maximum penalty is 18 months' imprisonment plus fines. Survivors told SBS the law does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Gender identity is a protected attribute under Queensland's anti-discrimination law, with state protections for sexuality and gender identity introduced in 2002. Transgender and intersex Queenslanders can update government records and birth certificates: the formal divorce requirements for such updates were repealed in 2018, and the surgery requirements were repealed in 2024. Since 1 September 2021 Queensland formally includes the 'X' non-binary option on marriage certificates, forms and documents alongside male and female.

Healthcare access for trans minors is the sharpest adverse measure in force. Queensland's Health Minister Tim Nicholls halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria in January 2025, formalised by a 28 January 2025 Queensland Health directive that exempts existing Queensland Children's Gender Service patients. Equality Australia called Queensland an 'outlier state'. The ban remains legally contested, and affected families report private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection, nearly $2,000 in one case.

Queensland's criminal and relationship law is comparatively permissive. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991 and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised; the age of consent was equalised to 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, Queensland being the last Australian jurisdiction to do so, replacing section 208's penalty of up to 14 years for anal sex involving a person under 18. A 2017 law expunging criminal records of men convicted of consensual homosexual acts took effect on 30 June 2018, and the gay panic defence was abolished in 2017. Same-sex couples may enter a civil partnership under state law or live in an unregistered de facto relationship recognised since 2002, and may become parents through adoption, foster care, altruistic surrogacy and, for lesbian couples, IVF, with adoption eligibility open since 11 November 2016.
tangentialFactors:
Queensland's 2020 conversion-practice ban was the first of its kind in Australia, but survivors told SBS the prohibition does not extend to informal, non-healthcare settings, leaving a gap between the statute and practice on the ground.

The January 2025 public-system treatment pause places Queensland at odds with other Australian jurisdictions on youth gender care; Equality Australia described the state as an 'outlier state'. The measure's contested legal status means its durability over a visit window is not settled.

Federal litigation over the exclusion of trans women from services continues to develop alongside Queensland's own vilification reforms, so a visitor may encounter both state Criminal Code vilification exposure and federal sex-discrimination remedies depending on the forum.
localsOnly:
Queensland residents can update government records and birth certificates without divorce or surgery requirements, both formal hurdles having been repealed in 2018 and 2024 respectively, and can obtain documents carrying an 'X' marker since 1 September 2021.

Serious vilification is now a Criminal Code offence in Queensland carrying up to three years' imprisonment, enforceable by state police rather than through the anti-discrimination complaint route, and the Queensland Human Rights Commission retains a discrimination-complaint function under the amended Act.

Residents under 18 newly presenting with gender dysphoria cannot access puberty blockers or hormones through Queensland Health under the January 2025 directive, while existing Queensland Children's Gender Service patients are exempt; families pursuing private treatment report costs running to hundreds of dollars per injection.

State law provides civil partnerships and recognised de facto status for same-sex couples, with adoption, foster care, altruistic surrogacy and IVF available to same-sex couples, IVF eligibility for lesbian couples dating from the state's parented-law framework and adoption eligibility open since 11 November 2016.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement of stronger gender-diverse discrimination protections rests on the record held here rather than a live page; the underlying page was not reachable at the time of writing.

The Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 rewrite described by the commission and the 29 April 2024 commencement reported by Star Observer are treated as related but separately sourced items; whether the bill and the commenced amendments are the same instrument is unresolved in the sources.

The legal challenge to the January 2025 youth treatment directive is described as ongoing but no court, filing date or outcome is given in the inventory; the directive's status at any future visit date is unresolved.

No Queensland-specific incident of violence against a trans person, and no Queensland-specific border or airport screening treatment of trans travellers, appears in the inventory; absence here is not sourced evidence of safety.
